chunks: As for what Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated, from Musa ibn al-Hasan, from Abu al-Qasim ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Hammad al-Kufi, from Bashir, from Abu Maryam al-Ansari, who said:

I was with Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام in a garden belonging to him when the time for salat (prayer) came. He drew up a bucket for wudu (ablution) from a well of his, and on it there came out a piece of dry feces, so he tilted off its top and performed wudu (ablution) with what remained.

This report may also bear two possibilities: one of them is what we mentioned in the two previous reports, that what is meant by al-rakiyy is the reservoir in which there is abundant water; and the second is that the feces is understood to have been the feces of an animal whose meat is eaten, and that does not render the water impure in any case.

key_terms.الصَّلَاةُ: salat (prayer), whose time had arrived in the report
key_terms.الْمَاءُ الْكَثِيرُ: abundant water, indicating a quantity not easily affected by impurity
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), the ritual washing intended with the water
key_terms.رَكِيٍّ: a well or water reservoir from which the water was drawn
key_terms.عَذِرَةٍ يَابِسَةٍ: dry feces found on the drawn bucket
key_terms.لَا يُنَجِّسُ الْمَاءَ: does not render the water impure

ai.seo_question: Does dry feces falling into well water make the water impure for wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This report describes Imam Abu ʿAbd Allah عليه السلام drawing water for wudu (ablution) from a well or water source in which a piece of dry feces appeared, yet he used the remaining water. The accompanying explanation presents legal possibilities showing why the water was not considered impure, making the narration relevant to rulings on ritual purity and wudu (ablution).
